name: ICIJ Prophecies
purpose: Collaborative data-checking application where a team is served records to verify or correct, with task assignment, progress tracking, inter-annotator comparison and a record of who checked what.
journalism_use_case: The step nobody builds and everybody needs: when an extracted dataset of 50,000 records must be human-verified before publication, Prophecies turns that into assigned tasks with progress tracking and an audit trail — rather than a shared spreadsheet where nobody knows what has been checked.
pros: Addresses the real bottleneck in data-driven investigation — human verification at scale — which no other tool in this catalogue tackles directly
Inter-annotator comparison surfaces disagreement between checkers, which is how you find systematically ambiguous records rather than discovering them after publication
Built by ICIJ for its own cross-border projects, so the collaboration model assumes distributed teams in different time zones and organisations
Produces an audit trail of who verified which record, which is exactly what you want when a published figure is challenged
cons: Small project with limited external community, so deployment support is thin and you will read source
Requires a defined verification task: it is for checking records against a rule, not for open-ended analysis, so framing the task well is the prerequisite and takes thought
Yet another platform to deploy alongside your document and search systems, and the value only appears when there is a large verification job to do
Development cadence follows ICIJ's project needs rather than a public roadmap
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: the repository is live and non-archived under ICIJ maintenance. ICIJ builds it for its own cross-border investigations, which is the most relevant provenance available for a collaborative-verification tool.
assessment: Worth piloting when you have a verification job large enough to need coordination — which arrives sooner than teams expect, typically the first time an extraction produces thousands of records that must be checked before publication. For your profile the alternative is a disciplined spreadsheet with an assignment column, which works up to a point and then silently fails; Prophecies is what you deploy when it has failed once. The audit trail is the durable benefit.
maintenance_evidence: Verified via the GitHub API 2026-11-17 as live and non-archived under ICIJ's maintenance, with activity following the organisation's project cycles rather than a public release cadence. Classified stable-low: institutionally maintained for internal use, published openly.
licence: AGPL-3.0 (project licensing — confirm from the repository licence file)
licence_restrictions: Copyleft would apply to a modified hosted instance; immaterial for internal deployment.
costs: No fee. A Django-class deployment plus a database — modest. The dominant cost is the human verification labour it organises, which it makes visible rather than reduces. Estimate.
privacy: Self-hosted; records under verification stay internal. The assignment data reveals who in your team is working on what, which is minor but worth knowing in a multi-organisation collaboration.
alternatives: A structured spreadsheet with assignment and status columns, which works for smaller jobs
Datasette with a custom form plugin for a lighter bespoke verification interface
Label Studio for annotation-oriented verification tasks
summary: Collaborative data-checking application where a team is served records to verify or correct, with task assignment…

name: juditha
purpose: Fast lookup service for canonical entity names, built to check whether a string matches a known entity in a reference dataset such as OpenSanctions or a FollowTheMoney collection.
journalism_use_case: High-speed name checking inside an ingest pipeline: as documents are processed, test every extracted name against a reference set of sanctioned entities and known companies, so flagged documents surface immediately rather than after a separate screening pass.
pros: Designed for the pipeline position where screening actually belongs — at ingest, not as a later batch — which shortens the time between receiving documents and knowing which matter
Built by DARC, the same organisation maintaining OpenAleph, so it fits coherently with the FollowTheMoney and OpenSanctions stack
Narrow scope done well: fast canonical-name lookup rather than a general matching framework, which makes it comprehensible and replaceable
Self-hosted, so the names you check are not disclosed to anyone
cons: Very small project with minimal community, so documentation is thin and you are reliant on the maintainer's context — a real adoption cost
Name lookup is not entity resolution: a match is a string correspondence requiring adjudication, and treating it as identification would produce false allegations
Tightly coupled to the FollowTheMoney and OpenSanctions ecosystem, so its value depends on having adopted that stack
Maintenance follows one organisation's needs, so continuity depends on DARC's priorities
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: the repository is live and non-archived under DARC's maintenance, in the same organisation that maintains OpenAleph. No independent deployment verified.
assessment: Integrate it if you have adopted the OpenAleph and OpenSanctions stack and want screening at ingest — the pipeline position is the right one and the component is small enough to understand. For your profile the caution is interpretive rather than technical: a name match at ingest is a flag for human attention, and the pipeline should route flagged documents to a reviewer rather than labelling them. Outside that ecosystem, rigour plus RapidFuzz over your own reference list does the same job.
maintenance_evidence: Verified via the GitHub API 2026-11-17 as live and non-archived under DARC's maintenance. The project is small with limited release history, and its continuity depends on one organisation's internal needs — classified Uncertain rather than inferring health from the parent organisation's activity on other repositories.
licence: MIT (project licensing — confirm from the repository licence file)
model_or_data_licence: Reference data you load carries its own licence — OpenSanctions data is CC-BY-NC-4.0, which applies to this use.
licence_restrictions: Code permissive as published. The data licence is the operative restriction if you load OpenSanctions.
costs: No fee. A small service plus the reference dataset. Negligible infrastructure. Estimate.
privacy: Self-hosted lookups disclose nothing externally — the key property for screening names from a confidential document set.
alternatives: yente for a fuller self-hosted matching API over the same data
rigour plus RapidFuzz over your own reference list for a dependency-light equivalent
nomenklatura for batch resolution rather than inline lookup
summary: Fast lookup service for canonical entity names, built to check whether a string matches a known entity in a reference dataset…
oss_detail: Open-source code, data or models you load carrying their own terms, some non-commercial

name: HURIDOCS preserve
purpose: Service that captures and preserves web content referenced in human-rights documentation, producing screenshots, text and media copies linked to records in a documentation system such as Uwazi.
journalism_use_case: Preserving the online evidence a documentation collection cites: when a Uwazi record references a social post or a government page, preserve captures it so the record remains verifiable after the source is deleted — which, for human-rights and conflict documentation, is routine rather than exceptional.
pros: Closes the specific gap between documentation and preservation: a citation in a records system is worthless once the source disappears, and this makes capture part of the documentation workflow rather than an afterthought
Integrates with Uwazi, so for teams on that stack preservation becomes automatic rather than a discipline someone must remember
Built by HURIDOCS for human-rights documentation, where source deletion and takedown are expected rather than incidental
Self-hosted, so captured evidence stays under your control
cons: Narrow and ecosystem-coupled: its value is largely tied to Uwazi, and outside that stack ArchiveBox or Scoop covers the same need more generally
Small project with limited community and documentation, so adoption outside HURIDOCS' context requires reading source
Captures are screenshots and media rather than WARC, so provenance is weaker than a browsertrix-crawler or Scoop capture
Maintenance follows one organisation's needs
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: the repository is live and non-archived under HURIDOCS' maintenance, designed to complement Uwazi. No independent deployment verified.
assessment: Integrate it if you run Uwazi — automatic preservation of cited sources is exactly the right workflow and the integration is the reason to choose it over a general archiver. Outside that stack, ArchiveBox or Scoop gives you stronger captures with a larger community, and the more important point transfers either way: preservation of cited online sources should be automatic at the moment of citation, not a task someone does later, because later the source is gone.
maintenance_evidence: Verified via the GitHub API 2026-11-17 as live and non-archived under HURIDOCS' maintenance. The project is small and maintained to support Uwazi rather than as a standalone product, so independent continuity cannot be assessed from metadata — classified Uncertain accordingly.
licence: MIT (project licensing — confirm from the repository licence file)
model_or_data_licence: n/a. Captured content remains the original publishers' copyright.
licence_restrictions: Permissive as published; confirm before redistribution.
costs: No fee. A small service plus storage proportional to captures. Estimate.
privacy: Self-hosted captures stay internal. Your capture requests are visible to the source sites, which for a social post means the platform sees the fetch.
alternatives: ArchiveBox for general self-hosted preservation with multi-format capture
Scoop for provenance-attested single-page captures
browsertrix-crawler for high-fidelity WARC capture of dynamic sources
summary: Service that captures and preserves web content referenced in human-rights documentation, producing screenshots…

name: CourtListener
purpose: Platform and public database of US federal and state court opinions, dockets and filings, with full-text search, citation analysis, alerts and a comprehensive REST API, plus the RECAP archive of PACER documents.
journalism_use_case: The primary route into US litigation: search dockets and filings across courts, set alerts on a case or a party, and pull documents through the API — including the RECAP archive, which holds PACER filings that would otherwise cost money per page to retrieve.
pros: The RECAP archive is the standout: PACER charges per page, and RECAP makes previously purchased filings free, which materially changes what court reporting is affordable
Comprehensive API with alerts, so monitoring a case or a litigant is automatable rather than a manual check — the basis of a genuine court beat
AGPL-3.0 (licence verified in session 1 by reading the text) and operated by a non-profit whose mission is open legal data, so the continuity incentives align with yours
Citation analysis and the eyecite integration mean you can follow precedent and find related filings systematically
cons: US only, so it is irrelevant outside that jurisdiction except where a US case touches your story
Coverage is uneven: state-court coverage is far thinner than federal, and RECAP only holds what someone has already purchased and contributed — so absence of a filing means nothing
Self-hosting the platform is a serious undertaking (Django, PostgreSQL, Elasticsearch, substantial storage) and almost never the right choice given the public service exists
API rate limits and terms apply, and sustained heavy use should be discussed with the operator rather than assumed
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: session 1's a1disc/notes.md independently recorded 'courtlistener AGPL-3.0' after reading the licence text, resolving a NOASSERTION. Free Law Project's operation of CourtListener and RECAP is well documented and extensively used in US legal and investigative journalism.
assessment: Adopt the service (not the self-hosted platform) if any of your work touches US courts — the API plus alerts is the foundation of a court beat, and RECAP's economics are decisive. For your profile the practical note is to contribute back: the RECAP extension uploads filings you purchase, which both reduces cost for others and builds the archive you depend on. Treat gaps in coverage as gaps, not as evidence that no filing exists.
maintenance_evidence: Verified via the GitHub API 2026-11-17 as live and non-archived under Free Law Project's maintenance, with continuous development supporting an operating public service. Session 1 verified the AGPL-3.0 licence by reading the text. The operating service is the stronger maintenance signal.
licence: AGPL-3.0 (verified in session 1 by reading the licence text, resolving a GitHub NOASSERTION)
model_or_data_licence: Court opinions are generally public records; API terms govern bulk access and were not itemised in this survey.
licence_restrictions: AGPL-3.0 on the platform code. API terms and rate limits govern use of the service — check before heavy automated use.
costs: Free to use the public service and API within limits; bulk access terms not verified in this survey. PACER itself charges per page, which RECAP mitigates. Self-hosting would be a substantial infrastructure and storage commitment and is not recommended. Estimate.
privacy: Queries go to CourtListener, disclosing which cases and parties you are researching to a non-profit operator — low risk, but non-zero if the subject is sensitive. Self-hosting is impractical, so Tor is the realistic mitigation if query privacy matters.
alternatives: PACER directly, at per-page cost
juriscraper for scraping court sites not covered by CourtListener
National court portals for non-US jurisdictions
blockers: US jurisdiction only; state-court and RECAP coverage is incomplete
summary: Platform and public database of US federal and state court opinions, dockets and filings, with full-text search…

name: Juriscraper
purpose: Library of scrapers for US federal and state court websites, retrieving opinions, oral arguments and docket information in a normalised format, maintained per court.
journalism_use_case: Monitoring courts that CourtListener does not cover well, or building your own alerting on a specific court's filings — the per-court scraper model means you can add a court that matters to your beat rather than waiting for coverage.
pros: Per-court scraper architecture is the right design for a fragmented jurisdiction landscape, and the normalised output means courts become comparable
Maintained by the organisation that depends on it operationally for CourtListener, so the scrapers are exercised daily against real sites
BSD-family licence with a long history and active maintenance, so it is a dependency you can build on
Adding a court is a contained task, so extending coverage to a court on your beat is realistic rather than a project
cons: Court websites change constantly, so scraper breakage is continuous — the maintenance burden is intrinsic and visible in the project's issue flow
US only, and the architecture encodes US court conventions, so adapting it to another jurisdiction would be a substantial rewrite
Engineer-facing with no interface, so it is infrastructure for a monitoring system you build
For most purposes CourtListener's API gives you the same data without running scrapers, so Juriscraper is for the gaps
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: the repository is live and non-archived under Free Law Project's maintenance, with scrapers exercised in CourtListener's production ingest — which is the strongest form of evidence that they work.
assessment: Integrate it only to fill gaps CourtListener leaves, or to monitor a specific court with your own alerting. For your profile the general lesson is the one warn-scraper also teaches: per-jurisdiction scrapers are a continuing maintenance commitment, and the honest way to run them is to accept that cost explicitly or to rely on an organisation that already does — which, for US courts, is Free Law Project.
maintenance_evidence: Verified via the GitHub API 2026-11-17 as live and non-archived under Free Law Project's maintenance, with continuous per-court fixes driven by CourtListener's production requirements. Maintenance here means ongoing scraper repair rather than feature releases.
licence: BSD-2-Clause (project licensing — confirm from the repository licence file)
model_or_data_licence: Retrieved court records are generally public documents.
licence_restrictions: Permissive as published. Scraping court sites is ordinary access to public records, though rate limits and courtesy apply.
costs: No fee. Negligible compute; the real cost is scraper maintenance if you extend it. Estimate.
privacy: Your scraping is visible to the court websites, which is unremarkable for public records.
alternatives: CourtListener's API, which covers most needs without running scrapers
Writing a single bespoke scraper for one court you care about
National court portals and their own alerting where available
summary: Library of scrapers for US federal and state court websites, retrieving opinions…

name: openstates-scrapers
purpose: Collection of scrapers covering US state legislatures, collecting bills, votes, legislators, committees and events into a normalised schema published via the Open States API and bulk downloads.
journalism_use_case: Tracking legislation across states: find every state where a similar surveillance or press-freedom bill has been introduced, who sponsored it and how it was voted — the comparative analysis that reveals a coordinated legislative campaign rather than a local initiative.
pros: Cross-state normalisation is what makes comparative legislative analysis possible, and model-bill tracking across states is a recurring and important story type
Covers sponsors, votes and committees rather than only bill text, so the political analysis (who pushed it, who voted how) is supported
Data is published via an API and bulk downloads, so you can use the output without running the scrapers
Open-source with institutional maintenance and a long operating history
cons: Fifty-plus jurisdictions means continuous scraper breakage, and coverage quality varies by state — some legislatures publish badly and the data reflects that
US only, and the architecture encodes US legislative structure
Normalisation inevitably loses state-specific procedural detail, so for a single-state story the original source is better
API terms and any limits were not verified in this survey
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: the repository is live and non-archived under Open States' maintenance. The project's data is used in civic-technology and journalism contexts, which is documented by the organisation.
assessment: Use the API and bulk data rather than running the scrapers, unless a state you care about is broken and you intend to fix it. For your profile the high-value application is model-bill detection: near-identical legislative text appearing across several states is strong evidence of a coordinated campaign, and this dataset plus a text-similarity comparison (datasketch or RapidFuzz) surfaces it systematically. Verify API terms before building a dependency.
maintenance_evidence: Verified via the GitHub API 2026-11-17 as live and non-archived under Open States' institutional maintenance, with continuous per-state scraper work supporting an operating data service. Maintenance means ongoing repair rather than releases.
licence: MIT (project licensing — confirm from the repository licence file)
model_or_data_licence: Collected legislative records are public documents; Open States' own data terms apply to the published API and bulk data and were not verified here.
licence_restrictions: Code permissive as published. Confirm the data terms before republishing bulk extracts.
costs: No fee for the code. API access terms and limits not verified in this survey. Running scrapers yourself is a continuing maintenance cost. Estimate.
privacy: Public legislative records; no privacy dimension beyond ordinary web access.
alternatives: Open States API and bulk downloads instead of running scrapers — the recommended path
LegiScan or similar commercial services for broader coverage at cost
National parliamentary open-data portals for non-US jurisdictions
blockers: US only; per-state coverage quality varies
summary: Collection of scrapers covering US state legislatures, collecting bills, votes, legislators…

name: Querido Diário
purpose: Collection of scrapers and a platform that gather Brazilian municipal official gazettes, extract their text and make them searchable across thousands of municipalities.
journalism_use_case: Searching thousands of municipal gazettes at once: contracts, appointments, emergency decrees and payments are published in local gazettes that nobody reads, and making them searchable turns an invisible record into a reportable one — for example finding the same contractor awarded emergency contracts across dozens of municipalities.
pros: Addresses a genuinely invisible public record: municipal gazettes are legally published and practically unread, so systematic search finds material no one has looked at
Civic-tech model with a large contributor community adding municipalities, which is how coverage of thousands of jurisdictions becomes feasible
Directly transferable architecture: the one-scraper-per-municipality pattern applies to any country with decentralised official publication, which is most of them
Open Knowledge Brasil's institutional maintenance plus community contribution gives it both direction and capacity
cons: Brazil-specific in coverage, so elsewhere it is a template rather than a resource
Thousands of scrapers means continuous breakage and uneven coverage, with the honest consequence that absence of a gazette for a municipality means nothing
Gazette text quality varies enormously — many are scanned PDFs of poor quality, so OCR errors propagate into search results
Running the full platform is a substantial undertaking; using the public service is the sensible path
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: the repository is live and non-archived under Open Knowledge Brasil's maintenance with a visible community-contribution model. The platform operates publicly, which is the relevant evidence.
assessment: Directly useful for Brazil and valuable everywhere as a model — the architecture is the transferable asset. For your profile, if you cover a country with decentralised official publication, this is the project to study before building: the per-jurisdiction scraper plus shared search pattern is proven, and the community-contribution model is how coverage scales beyond what one newsroom can maintain. Use the public service for Brazilian work rather than self-hosting.
maintenance_evidence: Verified via the GitHub API 2026-11-17 as live and non-archived under Open Knowledge Brasil's maintenance, with a community-contribution model adding and repairing municipal scrapers continuously. Maintenance means ongoing scraper work supporting an operating public service.
licence: MIT (project licensing — confirm from the repository licence file)
model_or_data_licence: Gazette content is official public record; the aggregated search service's terms were not verified here.
costs: No fee. Public service free to use. Self-hosting thousands of scrapers plus search is a major commitment. Estimate.
privacy: Public records; queries to the public service disclose your search terms to the operator.
alternatives: Building the equivalent for your own jurisdictions using this architecture — the more widely applicable use
egazette for Indian gazette collection with a similar purpose
National official-journal portals where centralised publication exists
blockers: Brazil-specific coverage; per-municipality coverage is uneven
summary: Collection of scrapers and a platform that gather Brazilian municipal official gazettes…
